newsitem.title: ITALY: Analysts see smooth takeoff for Aeroporti di Roma. [CORRECTED 12:32 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Analysts see smooth takeoff for Aeroporti di Roma. [CORRECTED 12:32 GMT]

text.p: Propelled by revenue from retail activities, Italian airport operator Aeroporti di Roma (ADR) should be a high flier on the Milan bourse, but it risks some turbulence from troubled state carrier Alitalia.
ADR, which runs Rome's Fiumicino and Ciampino airports, expects to make its market debut next Thursday or Friday. A public offer for the company that ended Wednesday was heavily oversubscribed.

"It's a very positive company with tremendous revenue upside from retail," said Andrew Light, a transport analyst from Salomon Brothers (corrects name of brokerage) in London. "ADR will be able to double its retail revenue in five years."
Analysts cautioned that ADR's success could be affected by the performance of Italy's financially strapped Alitalia, which is based in Rome, and by competition from the fast-growing Milan airports.
"Alitalia is a handicap. It could cause a dampening of growth potential," Light said.
Retail activities, the company's fastest-growing sector, grew 15 percent in 1996 to 255 billion lire ($146 million), but analysts say the airports' retail capacity is underdeveloped.
ADR now manages some 70 outlets rented out to boutiques, offices, shops, bars and restaurants mostly in Fiumicino.
Light noted that Gatwick airport in London, which is about the same size as Fiumicino, has 29,000 square metres devoted to retailing while the Roman airport has 17,000.

And ADR spends half as much on retailing per passenger compared with the British BAA, the oldest airport management authority in Europe to be quoted on the market, he added. "BAA has exhausted its retail space...at ADR not enough space has been devoted yet to retailing."
Analysts warn, however, that ADR's smooth cruising could be affected by the performance of ailing Alitalia.

As part of a recapitalisation plan approved by the European Union earlier this year, the Italian state carrier has promised to reduce its fleet of planes by 14 and cut some 27,000 flights a year, or 10 percent of operations, off its timetables.

"Alitalia is critical because it is the only airline (based) in Rome," Light said. "ADR will have to attract other airlines." But other analysts said any cuts that Alitalia might have to incur would have negative effects only in the short term.

"There is a risk of short-term disruption. Ultimately, if Alitalia doesn't carry, others will," Mike Powell, an analyst at Natwest Markets, said. He pointing in particular to Middle Eastern and African airlines which already have a foothold in the Rome airports.

Analysts also warn it may be difficult for Rome's airports to become a hub for international travel. Not only is Italy's capital not a natural transit point, but increasing competition could come from the Milan airports.

A two trillion lire capital improvement programme is under way at Milan's international Malpensa airport. The plan involves transferring all international flights and some domestic flights to Malpensa and sprucing up the airport with a doubled runway capacity, new terminal, expanded apron and cargo areas and other facilities.
Malpensa's expected capacity is 24 million passengers annually, which would equal ADR's passenger level for 1996.
"Malpensa is a newer airport and Milan has a stronger travel base," Light said. "And, Rome is not a credible connecting point," he added.
Aeroporti di Roma will be the fourth airport management authority in Europe to be quoted, after BAA and the companies that manage the Copenhagen and Vienna airports, respectively.

ADR boosted its net profits by 61 percent in 1996 to 90 billion lire and increased its turnover 11 percent to 1.16 trillion lire. The airports had traffic of more than 260,000 aircraft and 267,000 tonnes of freight.
The company, ranked fifth among European airport authorities in terms of number of passengers handled, aims to raise the capacity of Rome's airports to 30 million by the year 2000.
The public sale offer that ended on Wednesday was heavily oversubscribed, with 185,000 bidders applying for 170 million shares and institutional offers 21 times overbooked.
Strong demand for the 11,000-lire shares will likely lead to a green shoe option to lift the market stake and decrease the Italian industrial holding Iri stake in ADR to around 54 percent.
According to Powell, "the offer was very underpriced."
ADR is poised to cash in when thousands of Roman Catholics are expected to arrive in Rome for the Vatican's Holy Year celebrations in 2000. -- Rome newsroom +396 678 2501 ($ = 1743 Italian Lire)
